client: I just don't feel like myself since my dog passed away last month. Everything feels dull and empty, even things I used to enjoy like going for walks or watching TV. Part of me wonders if talking about it will even help - the pain feels too deep.
therapist: I hear how deeply you're missing your dog, and how that loss has made even simple pleasures feel empty right now. While your words describe this heavy dullness, I notice your voice sounds more rushed and higher than usual—almost like there's an urgency underneath the sadness. Would it feel okay to explore what that urgency might be about?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, very rapid speech

client:
I don't know why my voice sounds like that. Maybe it's because everyone keeps telling me I should be "moving on" by now, and I feel guilty that I'm not. But how am I supposed to just stop missing him? It's been three months and my apartment still feels so unbearably quiet without his little paws clicking on the floor. 

Part of me is scared that if I stop hurting, it means I didn't really love him enough. That urgency you're hearing... maybe it's me trying to prove something, even to myself? But that sounds ridiculous when I say it out loud.
therapist:
It makes complete sense that you'd feel this conflict between others' expectations and your very real grief—that pressure to "move on" while still feeling your dog's absence so profoundly. What stands out to me is how you're holding two truths at once: missing him deeply while also worrying what that pain means about your love—that doesn't sound ridiculous at all, it sounds like someone who loved deeply. 

Would it help to explore what "enough" love would look like to you in this situation? Because what I'm hearing is that your love for him was—and still is—very real.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client:
I don't know what "enough" love would look like...that's part of why this is so confusing. When people say "you gave him a good life," it makes me wonder if I really did enough while he was here. Maybe if I'd loved him enough, I wouldn't feel this guilty now. 

The idea that my love was real does help a little, but it's hard to hold onto when the grief still hurts this much months later. Shouldn't I be "over it" by now if my love was truly enough?
therapist:
Your voice sounds so full of urgency as you wrestle with these questions about "enough"—it's clear how much this matters to you. Grief doesn't follow a timeline, and the fact that it still hurts speaks to the depth of your bond, not any lack of love. 

What if we gently challenge that word "should"? Where does that expectation about being "over it" come from?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client:
I guess that "should" comes from seeing other people move on faster after losses. My sister seemed fine just a few months after our mom died, but here I am years later still crying sometimes. It makes me feel like I'm failing at grieving properly. 

The idea that grief doesn't have a timeline sounds nice, but in reality people do judge you when you're not "over it" when they think you should be. My coworkers definitely treat me differently when I get quiet around the anniversary dates.
therapist:
It sounds like you've internalized those external judgments about how grief "should" look, and it's left you feeling like you're somehow doing this wrong—especially when comparing yourself to others like your sister. Your voice sounds both quicker and heavier as you describe this, almost like you're carrying the weight of those expectations while also trying to explain yourself. 

What if we explore what "grieving properly" would actually mean for you—not for your coworkers or anyone else? Because grief isn't something we perform for others; it's how we honor what mattered to us.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client:
That actually makes me tear up a little. I've been so focused on how I *should* be grieving that I haven't even considered what would feel true for me. But part of me worries that if I stop performing grief the "right" way, people will think I didn't love my mom enough. 

It's confusing because some days I feel numb, and that scares me more than the sad days do. Shouldn't I be more devastated all the time?
therapist:
It sounds like you're caught between two fears—that feeling numb means you didn't care enough, and that others will judge you if your grief doesn't look how they expect. Your voice softened just now as you described this, which makes me wonder if part of you already knows there's no "right" way to grieve. 

What if we treated these numb moments not as failures, but as your mind's way of giving you small breaks from the pain? Grief isn't a performance—it's as unique as the love you shared.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, moderate-paced speech

client:
I know logically that grief isn't supposed to look a certain way, but it's hard to shake this pressure that I'm doing it wrong. When people ask how I'm holding up and I say "okay," I see their faces change like they're disappointed I'm not more of a wreck. 

Part of me wants to believe these numb moments are just breaks, but then I worry - what if I'm just avoiding the pain instead of properly processing it?
therapist:
I hear how exhausting it is to constantly monitor both your own grief and others' reactions to it—like you're being pulled in two directions at once. Your voice sounds quieter and flatter than usual as you describe this, almost like you're worn out from performing for those expectations. 

What if we reframe "avoiding" versus "processing"? Sometimes those numb moments aren't avoidance—they're simply part of the natural ebb and flow of grief. Could we explore what "properly processing" would actually look and feel like for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client:
I don't know... when you say "natural ebb and flow," it makes me feel like I'm doing grief wrong somehow. Like there's still a right way and I'm failing at it. The numb moments scare me because what if I'm just shutting down instead of actually dealing with things? 

It's hard to imagine what "properly processing" would feel like when everyone around me seems to expect either constant tears or this inspirational recovery story. Neither of those feels true to me.
therapist:
It sounds like even the idea of grief having an "ebb and flow" has become another standard you feel pressured to meet, when really there's no script for this. Your voice sounds both rushed and quiet right now—like you're trying to explain something fragile before it slips away. 

What if we set aside all the "shoulds" for a moment? What does your grief actually feel like in your body when you're not worrying about performing it for others?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: It's hard to describe... when I try to focus on my body, it's like there's this heavy weight pressing down on my chest. But at the same time, I feel this restless energy in my hands and legs, like I need to be doing something about it. That's why I keep trying to find the "right" way to grieve - because sitting with this feeling is unbearable.
therapist:
You're describing something so physically palpable—that push-pull between heaviness and restless energy. It makes sense that you'd want to "do something" with that intensity, especially when the alternative feels unbearable. 

What if we just notice that sensation together for a moment, without needing to fix or judge it? Where does that restless energy want to go when you let it move?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, fast speech

client:
I don't know... when I try to just notice the restlessness, it actually makes me more anxious. Like I'm failing at sitting with it properly. My chest gets tighter and I start thinking about all the things I should be doing instead. 

It's frustrating because part of me wants this to help, but another part just wants to scream and run away from sitting still with these feelings.
therapist:
It sounds like even the act of trying to notice these feelings brings up more tension—like there's no safe way to be with them without feeling like you're failing. That frustration comes through so clearly in your voice, which sounds higher and faster right now as you describe that urge to scream or run. 

Could we try something different? Instead of sitting with the feelings, what if we explored what that restlessness might need to express? Sometimes movement helps when stillness feels impossible.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client:
I don't know... moving around when I'm anxious just makes me feel more out of control. Last time I tried pacing, it made my heart race even worse and I ended up crying in the bathroom at work. 

But you're right that stillness feels like torture sometimes. It's like my body is screaming at me to do something, but everything I try makes it worse. I hate this trapped feeling.
therapist:
I hear how trapped you feel between these two impossible options—where moving makes the anxiety worse, but staying still feels unbearable. Your voice sounds both louder and higher right now, like your body is amplifying what your words are describing. 

What if we approach this differently? Instead of trying to fix or change these sensations, could we simply acknowledge how hard this is—how much your system is struggling right now? Sometimes naming the struggle can create a little space around it.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, moderate-paced speech
